questions.title: Miles per gallon from text input
questions.prompt:
Values typed into a text box arrive as **strings**. The starter code has two of them.

1. Convert both to numbers (the book uses `parseFloat()` for this).
2. Calculate miles per gallon (miles ÷ gallons).
3. Store the result **rounded to one decimal place** as a string in a constant named `mpg`, using the Number method `toFixed()`.
4. Log the message `Miles per gallon = 23.3` (built from `mpg` with string concatenation or a template literal).
hints: parseFloat("350") returns the number 350.
number.toFixed(1) returns a string with one digit after the decimal point.

questions.title: Find and fix the bugs
questions.prompt:
The `getAverage()` function in the starter code is supposed to return the average of an array of scores, but it has **two bugs**: one makes it skip a score, and one is a logic error in the math.

Fix the function so that:

```
getAverage([90, 80, 70])     // 80
getAverage([100])            // 100
getAverage([])               // 0   (no scores: return 0, not NaN)
```

Then handle the empty-array case shown above. Use `console.log()` to trace values if it helps — that's a debugging technique from the chapter.
hints: Arrays start at index 0. Which score does the loop never read?
Operator precedence: division happens before subtraction. Is the "- 1" needed at all?
Check scores.length === 0 before dividing.

questions.title: Countdown with an interval timer
questions.prompt:
The page shows a number of seconds. Using an **interval timer**:

1. Every **1 second**, subtract one from the number in `#seconds` and display the new value.
2. When it reaches `0`, **stop the timer** and put the text `Liftoff!` in `#message`.

Start the timer as soon as the page loads. (Checking this answer takes about 4 seconds while the timer runs.)
hints: setInterval(callback, 1000) returns a timer id; clearInterval(id) stops it.
Store the timer id in a variable the callback can see.
Read the count with parseInt(element.textContent) or keep it in a variable.

questions.title: Random die rolls and formatted prices
questions.prompt:
Write two functions:

1. `rollDie()` returns a random **whole number from 1 to 6**, each equally likely (like the PIG game in the chapter). Use the `Math` object.
2. `formatPrice(amount)` returns the amount as US currency with a dollar sign, comma separators and exactly two decimals:

```
formatPrice(1234.5)   // "$1,234.50"
formatPrice(7)        // "$7.00"
```
hints: Math.random() returns a number from 0 up to (not including) 1. Multiply, then use Math.floor().
The Internationalization API formats currency: new Intl.NumberFormat("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }).format(amount)
amount.toLocaleString("en-US", { style: "currency", currency: "USD" }) also works.

tests.name: rollDie() always returns a whole number from 1 to 6
tests.code:
for (let i = 0; i < 2000; i++) { const n = rollDie(); if (!Number.isInteger(n) || n < 1 || n > 6) return false; }
return true;

tests.name: rollDie() can return every value 1–6

questions.title: Validate a phone number and throw an error
questions.prompt:
Write a function `parsePhone(text)` that:

- Uses a **regular expression** to check that `text` matches the pattern `999-999-9999` (three digits, dash, three digits, dash, four digits — nothing before or after).
- If it does **not** match, **throws** an `Error` object whose message is `Invalid phone number`.
- If it matches, returns the 10 digits with the dashes removed.

```
parsePhone("555-123-4567")   // "5551234567"
parsePhone("5551234567")     // throws Error("Invalid phone number")
```

Then write a `try...catch` statement that calls `parsePhone("call me")` and logs the error's **message** to the console.
hints: A regex for a digit is \d; \d{3} means exactly three. Anchor the pattern with ^ at the start and $ at the end.
pattern.test(text) returns true or false.
throw new Error("Invalid phone number"); and in the catch block use error.message.
text.replace(/-/g, "") removes every dash.

tests.name: Throws an Error with message "Invalid phone number" for "5551234567"
tests.code: try { parsePhone("5551234567"); return false; } catch (e) { return e instanceof Error && e.message === "Invalid phone number"; }

tests.name: Rejects extra characters ("x555-123-4567" and "555-123-45678")
tests.code:
for (const bad of ["x555-123-4567", "555-123-45678", "555-12-34567"]) { try { parsePhone(bad); return false; } catch (e) { /* expected */ } }
return true;

questions.title: Task list saved in web storage
questions.prompt:
Build the core of the chapter's Task List application with **local storage**. The tasks are stored under the key `tasks` as a **JSON array of strings**. (In this sandbox, local storage already contains one task.)

1. When the page loads, read the tasks from local storage (use an empty array if there are none) and display each one as an `<li>` in `#task_list`.
2. When `#add_task` is clicked, add the text from `#task` (if it isn't blank) to the array, save the array back to local storage, redisplay the list, and clear the text box.

setup.css:
body { font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif; padding: 1em; }
#task_list li { padding: .2em 0; }

hints: localStorage.getItem("tasks") returns a string or null. JSON.parse() turns the string back into an array.
JSON.stringify(array) converts the array to a string for localStorage.setItem().
Write a displayTasks() function that clears the list (innerHTML = "") and adds an <li> for each task; call it on load and after adding.

tests.name: Shows the saved task when the page loads
tests.code:
const items = document.querySelectorAll("#task_list li");
return items.length === 1 && items[0].textContent.trim() === "Read chapter 14";

tests.name: Adding a task shows it in the list
Local storage holds both tasks as a JSON array
tests.code:
const saved = JSON.parse(localStorage.getItem("tasks"));
return Array.isArray(saved) && saved.length === 2 && saved[0] === "Read chapter 14" && saved[1] === "Practice regex";

tests.name: The text box is cleared after adding
A blank task is not added

questions.title: Array methods, a Set and a Map
questions.prompt:
The starter code has an array of order objects. Without writing any `for` loops, create:

1. `bigOrders` — an array of only the orders with a `total` of **100 or more** (use `filter()`).
2. `grandTotal` — the sum of every order's total (use `reduce()`).
3. `customers` — a **Set** of the unique customer names.
4. `totalsByCustomer` — a **Map** whose keys are customer names and whose values are that customer's combined order totals.
questions.starterCode:
const orders = [
  { customer: "Ana", total: 120 },
  { customer: "Ben", total: 45 },
  { customer: "Ana", total: 30 },
  { customer: "Cho", total: 210 },
  { customer: "Ben", total: 100 },
];
hints: orders.filter(order => order.total >= 100)
orders.reduce((sum, order) => sum + order.total, 0)
new Set(orders.map(order => order.customer))
For the Map, use forEach(): map.set(name, (map.get(name) || 0) + order.total)

tests.name: bigOrders has the 3 orders of 100 or more
customers is a Set of 3 names
tests.code: return customers instanceof Set && customers.size === 3 && customers.has("Ana") && customers.has("Ben") && customers.has("Cho");

tests.name: totalsByCustomer is a Map with Ana 150, Ben 145, Cho 210
tests.code: return totalsByCustomer instanceof Map && totalsByCustomer.get("Ana") === 150 && totalsByCustomer.get("Ben") === 145 && totalsByCustomer.get("Cho") === 210 && totalsByCustomer.size === 3;

questions.title: A class and a subclass
questions.prompt:
Inspired by the chapter's Trips application, write:

1. A class `Trip` whose constructor takes `destination`, `miles` and `gallons` and stores them as properties.
   - Add a **getter** named `mpg` that returns miles ÷ gallons rounded to one decimal place, as a **number**.
   - Add a method `toString()` that returns e.g. `Chicago: 23.3 mpg`.
2. A class `RoadTrip` that **extends** `Trip`, takes a fourth constructor argument `stops`, and overrides `toString()` to add the stops: `Denver: 25 mpg (3 stops)`. Call the parent's `toString()` with `super`.
hints: class Trip { constructor(destination, miles, gallons) { this.destination = destination; ... } }
A getter is written get mpg() { ... } and is read without parentheses: trip.mpg
Number((miles / gallons).toFixed(1)) gives a rounded number. Template literals help with toString().
class RoadTrip extends Trip { constructor(d, m, g, stops) { super(d, m, g); this.stops = stops; } }

tests.name: mpg is a getter, not a method
RoadTrip extends Trip
tests.code:
const r = new RoadTrip("Denver", 500, 20, 3);
return r instanceof Trip && r.stops === 3 && r.mpg === 25;

questions.title: Private state with a closure
questions.prompt:
Write a function `createCounter(start = 0)` that uses a **closure** to keep a private count. It returns an object with three methods:

- `increment()` adds one to the count and returns the new count.
- `reset()` sets the count back to the starting value.
- `getCount()` returns the current count.

The count must be **private**: the returned object must not have a property that holds it. Each call to `createCounter()` must make an independent counter.

```
const a = createCounter();     // default parameter: starts at 0
const b = createCounter(10);
a.increment();                 // 1
b.increment();                 // 11
a.getCount();                  // 1
```
hints: Declare let count = start; inside createCounter. The returned methods can still use it after createCounter returns — that is the closure.
Return an object literal: return { increment() { ... }, reset() { ... }, getCount() { ... } };

tests.name: Default start is 0 and increment() returns the new count
tests.code:
const c = createCounter();
return c.getCount() === 0 && c.increment() === 1 && c.increment() === 2;

tests.name: Counters are independent
reset() returns to the starting value
The count is private (only the three methods are exposed)

questions.title: Get JSON data with fetch() and async/await
questions.prompt:
Like the chapter's examples, this question uses the JSON Placeholder API. (This sandbox has no internet, so `fetch()` returns built-in sample data for users 1 and 2, and a **404** for any other user.)

Write an **async** function `getUserName(id)` that:

1. Uses the **Fetch API** with `await` to request `https://jsonplaceholder.typicode.com/users/` followed by the id.
2. If the response is **not OK** (check `response.ok`), returns the string `Unknown user`.
3. Otherwise converts the response body from JSON and returns the user's `name`.

Then call `getUserName(1)` and display the result in `#user_name`.

setup.css: body { font-family: Arial, Helvetica, sans-serif; padding: 1em; }

hints: const response = await fetch(url); — this only works inside an async function.
response.ok is false for a 404. await response.json() parses the body.
An async function returns a promise: getUserName(1).then(name => ...)
